wine.name: Sárhegy Olaszrizling
wine.grapes: Olaszrizling, the grape Austria calls Welschriesling, named alone on the label.
wine.sites: The Sár-hegy, the volcanic hill that rises above Gyöngyös: andesite, rhyolite tuff and andesite tuff, with loess on its southern foot and brown forest soils, open to the sun on every side, by the house's account.
wine.making: Aged in Hungarian oak after the harvest, and in some vintages fermented in it: about three months in 225 litre barrels for the 2023, twelve months in 500 litre casks for the 2022, as the house's listings give them. The oak sets this wine apart from the house's unoaked Mátra Olaszrizling.
wine.glass: Straw gold, with yellow apple, a smoky edge and cloves, cinnamon and vanilla from the oak; round and creamy in the mouth, its acidity holding the oak and the body in balance.
wine.ageing: Give it a year or two after release for the oak to settle into the wine, as one taster advised, then drink it over the next few years.
wine.serve: 10 to 12 degrees Celsius; no need to decant; a medium white wine glass.

records.table: Dubicz's Sárhegy Olaszrizling takes one of Hungary's most widely planted white grapes to the volcanic Sár-hegy above Gyöngyös and gives it time in oak. Yellow apple, a smoky edge and a creamy texture make it the fuller face of the grape; pour it cool, not icy.
records.story: The house's story is the story of a building. In 1901 growers around Gyöngyös and Visonta formed a co-operative of 256 shares to press and sell their wine together, and by the house's account it became a share company in 1905 and acquired the building known as the Borpalota, the Wine Palace. An architectural history of the palace finds that 1905 was its turning point, though no single year of building can be given. In 1934 an ancestor of the family that runs the house changed the old family surname, Dubicz, to Dunai, as the times expected. The cellar's ownership was abolished in 1946, as the house tells it, returned briefly to private hands and nationalised in 1951, to be run by a state wine company. The family bought the winery in 2003, and in 2016 it gave the winery the old name, Dubicz. The palace was restored from 2023. The Sár-hegy, the volcanic hill above the town, gives the house its hill wines, and the oak aged Olaszrizling is the fullest of them. Here one of Hungary's most widely grown white grapes meets oak, in a cellar that has made wine in the town for well over a century.

The Sár-hegy is a volcanic hill above Gyöngyös in the Mátra, not a site of the Eger or Tokaj districts.

records.table: Benedek Pince's Kékfrankos comes from a family cellar at Gyöngyöstarján in the Mátra foothills: Hungary's Blaufränkisch, fermented in tank for sour cherry and crisp acidity rather than oak. Serve it a little cool beside pork, sausage or a paprika stew.
records.story: Gyöngyöstarján is a wine village on the southern foothills of the Mátra, north west of Gyöngyös. The Benedek family's cellar there was built in 1947 by the great grandparents of the generation that runs the house, as the family tells it, and the estate was begun again after 1990, starting small and growing over the following decades. The family describes its aim as a small estate in harmony with nature. Its wines are built in two tiers: a basic series, fermented in tank, and single vineyard wines above it, among them an old vine Hárslevelű that its importers sell abroad. Kékfrankos is widely grown in the Mátra, and Magyar Bor has called the district a new home of the grape after the years of mass production under socialism; growers from small artisan cellars to large family wineries have turned back to it. In neighbouring Gyöngyöspata, growers formed the Pata Wine Community and made Kékfrankos their flagship, with a festival of their own from 2023. The Benedek Kékfrankos is a plain, honest example of that turn: the grape of Sopron, Eger and Szekszárd grown on the volcanic foothills. It answers the guest who takes the Mátra for white wine country alone.

wine.name: Hárslevelű
wine.grapes: Hárslevelű, the linden leaf white grape of Tokaj and of Debrő in the Eger district, named alone on the label.

records.table: Losonci is a small family estate at Gyöngyöspata, begun in 2004 and run with a natural hand: no cultured yeast, slow, cool ferments. Its Hárslevelű, the linden leaf grape of Tokaj, brings honey and blossom from red andesite tuff on the Mátra's slopes.
records.story: Losonci began in 2004, as Magyar Bor's register of wineries records, a small family estate at Gyöngyöspata on the western side of the Mátra. Its range is wide for its size: Rajnai Rizling, Olaszrizling, Zöldveltelini, Furmint, Hárslevelű, Kékfrankos and Cabernet Franc are among its grapes, and every wine is sold in bottle. The cellar works by a rule of its own, set down on the house's pages: no added enzymes, no cultured yeast, only a small starter of the vineyard's own yeasts, and slow fermentation in the cool. The vineyard lies north east of the village at 220 to 340 metres, on a south west facing slope of red clay and red andesite tuff, the volcanic rock of the Mátra, which drains fast and keeps the upper soil dry. Its village has become a meeting place of the Mátra's newer growers, whose Pata Wine Community took Kékfrankos as its flagship and began a festival of its own in 2023. Hárslevelű, named for its linden shaped leaf, is grown above all in Tokaj, where it partners Furmint, and it has its own designation at Debrő in the Eger district. Losonci's bottle shows the grape away from Tokaj, on Mátra tuff, made by a family that leaves the cellar alone.

wine.grapes: Irsai Olivér, a Hungarian white crossing bred at Kecskemét in 1930, named alone on the label.

records.table: Orange blossom and fresh grape rise from Bárdos és Fia's Irsai Olivér, the Mátra's spring white from a Nagyréde family cellar of 1999 whose name means Bárdos and Son. Fermented cool in steel, light and dry, it should be drunk very cold and young.
records.story: Bárdos és Fia began in 1999 as a family business at Nagyréde, a village of the Mátra district, as the house tells it, and its name, Bárdos and Son, says the rest. The family planted its own vineyard on brown forest soil, at narrow spacing, and its main plots lie within the bounds of the village. The range runs from light whites to a red made in memory of the house's late owner: a Cabernet Franc of the 2019 vintage, the serious red of the Mátra he had planned to make, by the house's account; his son carries the house on. Irsai Olivér itself is a young grape, a crossing bred at Kecskemét in 1930 and grown across Hungary for its Muscat scent, and the Mátra grows more of it than any other district, by Magyar Bor's account; Cserszegi Fűszeres is its later offspring. The house makes it as a varietal wine and also puts it, with Sauvignon Blanc, Tramini and Ottonel Muskotály, into My Mátra, a white cuvée it calls the district's new community wine. The Bárdos Irsai Olivér is the Mátra's early white in its simplest form: cold, scented and gone by the next summer.

records.table: In 2017 the founder of Szőke Mátyás, a family cellar at Gyöngyöstarján, became Hungary's Winemaker of the Year, the first from the Mátra. The house's Mátrai Irsai Olivér is the district's summer white: light, dry and grapey, with lively acidity.
records.story: The family has made wine at Gyöngyöstarján since the 1970s, as the house tells it: its head, an engineer by training, took up winemaking in earnest then, and his son, trained as a winemaker, later joined him in the cellar, so the house carries both their names, family name first in the Hungarian order. The family vineyards lie around the village on the Mátra's southern foothills, among them Hajnal-hegy and Száraz-völgy, where the house grows a semi sweet Muscat Ottonel it counts among its flagship wines. In 2017 the Hungarian Wine Academy named the founder Winemaker of the Year, chosen from the nominations of hundreds of sommeliers, restaurateurs and other professionals, and he was the first from the Mátra in the award's history. The house is known for a broad range: Chardonnay, Muscat Ottonel, Irsai Olivér and Merlot are named among its wines, and it calls Peres Cuvée, a barrique aged Cabernet Sauvignon and Cabernet Franc, its flagship. The grape in this bottle, bred at Kecskemét in 1930 and grown across Hungary for its Muscat scent, is the Mátra's light white of spring and summer. This bottle is the house's everyday white, and a door into a cellar whose founder put the Mátra on the national map.

report: A rename of the wine is proposed, house and key kept: the house's own site calls Peres Cuvée (Cabernet Sauvignon and Cabernet Franc in barrique) its flagship, and its vineyard page counts the semi sweet Muscat Ottonel from Száraz-völgy among its flagship wines. Either would also end the plan's doubling of Irsai Olivér with Bárdos és Fia; the lint binds the wine's name to Irsai Olivér until plan.json changes.

The house's full name is Szőke Mátyás & Zoltán; the son is living and is not named in prose. The founder's status is unknown (one award list marks his entry with a dagger that no source explains), so he is treated as living and named only as the house.
The Trade Magazin source's address and title carry the founder's name, which is also the house's name; the checker may prefer to keep Daily News Hungary alone with the house's own pages.
Founded is empty: the house says only the 1970s. The award of 2017 and the first from the Mátra rest on Daily News Hungary and Trade Magazin; the award's age of 27 years is left out.
The Hajnal-hegy, Kisdomb and Száraz-völgy sites rest on the house's vineyard page and a Bor és Piac article; Kisdomb is left out for want of a second source.

The label term Szőke Mátyás & Zoltán carries the son's first name, as the house's own name does; the read together agent may prefer to cut it.
